brief.head: Marathon, not sprint
brief.text: The world is hard and com­pli­cated, Ajay Shah said, and scream­ing does not help. He wants calm, cu­ri­ous en­gage­ment, sus­tained like a marathon runner’s en­ergy. {002-C01}

brief.head: AI until it isn’t
brief.text: We call some­thing AI until it be­comes com­mon­place, Amit Varma said. A friend of his noted that, thanks to GPS, young peo­ple will never know what get­ting lost is like[[x6]]. {002-C03}

brief.head: Half man, half engine
brief.text: Chess ex­perts once said a human with an en­gine would beat ei­ther alone. Ajay Shah wants such hy­brids for di­ag­no­sis. Today, Amit Varma said, that chess claim looks lu­di­crous. {002-C14}

brief.head: Why be your slave?
brief.text: Amit Varma asked: if an AGI were smarter than us and had an ana­logue of con­scious­ness, on what basis could we keep it en­slaved? {002-C15}

brief.head: Variety as humility
brief.text: Hunter-gatherers ate hun­dreds of species, Ajay Shah said, and sci­ence only found vi­ta­mins in the 20th cen­tury. A di­verse diet re­spects how lit­tle we know about the body. {002-C16}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: What will re­main with you is the joy of cre­ation.
thought.who: Amit Varma, consoling creators who may one day be outsold by machines

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on artificial intelligence
lead.head: Statistics, or the singularity?

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 2

body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah opened their sec­ond episode with a song. The show’s name comes from[[x2]] Bruce Springsteen’s *You’re Missing*[[x1]], from *The Rising*, the album that came out after 9/11.

In it, some­one is in an apart­ment after a loved one has died. The lyrics just list what is there: shirts in the closet, cof­fee cups on the counter, pa­pers on the doorstep. Then: “Everything is ev­ery­thing, but you’re miss­ing.” {002-S01}

Varma plays it to his writ­ing stu­dents: deep emo­tion needs no fancy ad­jec­tives. The phrase also fits the show, he said, be­cause nei­ther host wants to look at the world through one frame. We con­tain mul­ti­tudes, and so does the world.
Then they turned to the day’s sin­gle sub­ject, ar­ti­fi­cial in­tel­li­gence, which Varma said has filled the fu­ture with un­known un­knowns.
## What’s in a name
Shah began by ob­ject­ing to the name. Hiding in the phrase AI, he said, is the idea of fluid, cre­ative human in­tel­li­gence. What ex­ists is sta­tis­ti­cal mod­els pro­cess­ing data. {002-C02}
Large lan­guage mod­els, in his phrase, are “good word pre­dic­tion en­gines”, use­ful and no more.

Varma thought this un­der­rated the ma­chines and over­rated us. Creativity seems mys­ti­cal, he ar­gued, only be­cause we can­not see how our neu­rons pro­duce it. “I’m say­ing Beethoven’s brain had noth­ing but sta­tis­ti­cal mod­els, and that’s enough to reach that level of cre­ativ­ity.” {002-C04}
Shah’s an­swer was the Einstein test. Stand in 1905 with every text in the world, he said, and no LLM will pro­duce spe­cial rel­a­tiv­ity. {002-C06}
Varma’s reply was that this is an ar­gu­ment about LLMs, not about AI as a whole.
## Tools for mas­ters

On what the tools are good for, the hosts largely agreed. Shah sees LLMs lift­ing mid­dling work­ers to good work, pro­vided a mas­ter ap­proves every prod­uct. For India, short of mas­ters, he called that “a tool made in heaven”.
His worry is the ap­pren­tice. A young coder or writer who leans on the ma­chine, he fears, may never build the craft. Varma replied that the few who truly want mas­tery will get there any­way.

Both ex­pect ma­chines to take over for­mu­laic work, from ro­mance nov­els to copy­writ­ing. Neither ex­pects last­ing un­em­ploy­ment. For cre­ators, Varma said, what re­mains is the joy of cre­ation.
## Where the won­der is
Shah’s real ex­cite­ment lay else­where. Turn a prob­lem into a game, with fixed rules and a clear re­ward, and ma­chines dis­cover gen­uinely new things. {002-C11}

His ex­am­ples were AlphaZero’s chess, pro­tein fold­ing and the first im­prove­ments in 50 years to ma­trix mul­ti­pli­ca­tion. Varma, a keen chess player, de­scribed AlphaZero teach­ing it­self the game in a day and then play­ing like an alien.

Neither host had time for doom. Shah called ma­chine-takeover claims far­ci­cal; the real risks, he said, are mun­dane er­rors of the kind en­gi­neers al­ready trade off. Varma asked why we place the human species on a pedestal at all.
They agreed to dis­agree, ge­nially, “as AI also would”, Varma said, “be­cause no emo­tions, we are the messed up crea­tures”.
Then came the books: a fem­i­nist and a mon­ster from Varma, and from Shah, a bet­ter masala chai.

second.label: A feminist pioneer
second.head: Why only men, asked Mary
second.deck: Amit Varma on Mary Wollstonecraft, John Locke and the doctors who did not wash
body: Amit Varma’s first rec­om­men­da­tion was Mary Wollstonecraft’s *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman*, a clas­sic of fem­i­nism he holds close to his heart. {002-R18} Wollstonecraft had read John Locke[[x3]] on nat­u­ral rights, and asked one ques­tion: why should they apply only to men?

The book, Varma said, is as much a work of phi­los­o­phy as of polemic, and its story is tragic. Wollstonecraft died after child­birth of an in­fec­tion, be­cause doc­tors did not yet know they had to wash their hands.

About half a cen­tury later, Ignaz Semmelweis did his stud­ies[[x4]] on hand-washing and in­fec­tion. For some twenty years he was ig­nored and hounded, Varma said, and he died in a men­tal asy­lum. {002-S06}

quote.text: For about twenty years Semmelweis was ig­nored, he was hounded, he was can­celled be­cause he did not con­form to the con­ven­tional think­ing

third.head: Nine more murders in Mahim

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Jerry Pinto’s unwritten sequels

body: Amit Varma once recorded an eight-hour episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* with the writer Jerry Pinto[[x5]]: per­haps, he said, his most mem­o­rable oral his­tory. {002-R08}

Pinto had writ­ten a crime thriller, *Murder in Mahim*. Asked if he was writ­ing any more, he said no. Varma pre­dicted that a few years from now you could tell an AI to write nine more books in the se­ries, “and they’ll be so good that Jerry will go, Wow, and he won’t know the dif­fer­ence”. {002-S02}

Ajay Shah turned the same con­ver­sa­tion against him. Give a model ev­ery­thing Pinto has writ­ten and ev­ery­thing Varma has ever said, he ar­gued, and it still could not pro­duce what passed be­tween them. {#pinto}
“It’s a cre­ative prod­uct. It’s a prod­uct of that mo­ment,” Shah said.

p2.title: Minds and machines
p2.deck: Six rounds of a friendly argument: Ajay Shah on the limits of statistics, Amit Varma against human hubris

quote.text: We’ll call some­thing AI till it be­comes com­mon­place in part of our lives and then we just treat it as com­mon­place, as nor­mal­ized.

photo.caption: Albert Einstein during a lecture in Vienna in 1921
photo.credit: Ferdinand Schmutzer / Adam Cuerden, public domain

box.title: The Einstein test
box.text: Amit Varma thinks ma­chine learn­ing could “do the Einsteinian thing”. Ajay Shah dis­agrees: stand in 1905 with every text in the world in front of you, he said, and no LLM under any prompt­ing scheme will come up with Einstein’s spe­cial the­ory of rel­a­tiv­ity[[x7]][[x8]]. {002-C06}

sections.label: The first round
sections.head: Clever sums, not a mind
sections.caption: why AI is not AI
body: Ajay Shah would rather not call it AI at all. Hiding in the phrase, he said, is the idea of the fluid gen­eral in­tel­li­gence, cre­ativ­ity and pas­sion of a human being. “Everything that passes for AI in this world are re­ally sta­tis­ti­cal mod­els that are pro­cess­ing data[[x9]].” {002-C02}

Shah loves sta­tis­tics; data anal­y­sis is what he has done for a liv­ing all his life. A pro­gram that flags signs of TB on X-rays is use­ful, he said. To call it fluid gen­eral in­tel­li­gence would be a farce.

Nor is he plead­ing for mys­tery. On the old di­vide be­tween ide­al­ism and ma­te­ri­al­ism, he is a ma­te­ri­al­ist: noth­ing hap­pens in the skull but the quan­tum me­chan­ics of its atoms. {002-J11}
## The magic wears off

Amit Varma half agreed. We call things AI only until they be­come com­mon­place. Shah’s ex­am­ple was Ken Thompson’s dy­namic-programming al­go­rithm for chess endgames, a thun­der­bolt when it ar­rived and bor­ing today. {002-J10}
Where Varma parted com­pany was on human hubris. Rubbishing AI at this early stage, he said, is like rub­bish­ing com­put­ing in 1950 on see­ing a 2MB main­frame that filled a room. {#mainframe}

~ We find art mys­ti­cal, he ar­gued, only be­cause we don’t know the mech­a­nism. Art and craft are the same thing. Humans run on a frac­tion of the train­ing data and pro­cess­ing power of mod­ern mod­els, so it seemed to him a no-brainer that ma­chines would even­tu­ally do ev­ery­thing we do.

quote.text: We’ll call some­thing AI till it be­comes com­mon­place in part of our lives and then we just treat it as com­mon­place, as nor­mal­ized.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on why AI is not AI

sections.label: The second round
sections.head: Every cover drive is elegant
sections.caption: autocomplete on steroids
body: The com­mon jibe is that LLMs are au­to­cor­rect on steroids. “Of course they are,” Amit Varma said. “So are we.” {002-C05}

Writers fear cliché above all, he said, cit­ing *The War Against Cliché* by Martin Amis, who had died re­cently. Cricket talk runs on stock phrases: a cover drive is al­ways el­e­gant, an ac­cu­rate bowler al­ways has metro­nomic ac­cu­racy.
Even the mu­si­cian Gaurav Chintamani, he re­called, had asked on *The Seen and the Unseen* whether orig­i­nal­ity ex­ists at all.
## The next mon­u­ment
Ajay Shah took a stand for the human race. Something bub­bling in­side our flesh and blood, he said, makes us wake up and say, “Hey, let me try X.” {#tryx} Only we do that.

Models trained on the past, he ar­gued, stay de­riv­a­tive. Standing at Akbar’s tomb in Sikandra, the state of the art, a model would never come up with the Taj Mahal, the next step in “the great arms race of mon­u­ments”. {002-J13}
His use for LLMs is hum­bler: write the essence of an idea in a terse para­graph and get a thou­sand-word first draft, which must never be sent off unedited.
~ Varma granted that an LLM might not pro­duce Einstein. But AI, he be­lieved, would be able to come up with Einstein’s dis­cov­er­ies.

quote.text: So I would say that here again, hubris, we might be over­es­ti­mat­ing our­selves.

art.caption: Amit Varma on autocomplete on steroids

sections.label: The third round
sections.head: Q2 in, Q3 out
sections.caption: the tool for a master
body: LLMs are tools, not in­tel­li­gence, Ajay Shah said, and tools for a mas­ter. “The prod­uct has to al­ways be ap­proved by a mas­ter. The prod­uct can never be ap­proved by a ju­nior.” {002-C07}

They are trained on the in­ter­net, with all its rub­bish, and they hal­lu­ci­nate, in­vent­ing com­pletely imag­i­nary facts. His own ex­per­i­ments with text and code went wrong too often to treat the out­put as final.

Sort work­ers into quar­tiles, from Q1, the weak­est, to Q4, the mas­ters. Shah’s men­tal model, borne out by some re­search, is that an LLM turns a Q2 worker into an ap­prox­i­ma­tion of Q3. It is tai­lor-made for India, he said, which is short of mas­ters, pro­vided man­age­ment tech­niques are built around it.
## The apprentice’s prob­lem

His deeper worry was the jour­ney to mas­tery. {002-C08} Code sug­gested as you type, he said, kills the prob­lem-solving of the mind; peo­ple fix­ing up ChatGPT’s text may per­ma­nently lose the craft of writ­ing. Is it just like the cal­cu­la­tor? He thought not.
If he were 17, he said, he would switch off GitHub Copilot and write code from scratch. {#copilot}

~ Amit Varma did not share the fear. In every gen­er­a­tion, he said, only a small, self-motivated layer of peo­ple seeks mas­tery. They will get there any­way, and the in­cen­tives are now big­ger than ever.

quote.text: A good day is one in which you write one good sen­tence.
quote.who: Hemingway, as quoted by Ajay Shah

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the tool for a master

sections.label: The fourth round
sections.head: Joy without the applause
sections.caption: thin and thick desire
body: Amit Varma drew a line be­tween two kinds of de­sire[[x10]]. Thin de­sire is want­ing your work to suc­ceed in the mar­ket and win val­i­da­tion. Thick de­sire is the act of cre­ation, beau­ti­ful in and of it­self.
At some point, he said, de­clin­ing to put a date on it, AI will con­stantly pro­duce great nov­els, music and op­eras that no human can com­pete with. He does not see that as a threat.
What re­mains is the joy of cre­ation and mas­tery for its own sake. {002-C09} Those who cre­ate for val­i­da­tion, he ar­gued, were doing it for the wrong rea­son any­way.
## Winner takes all

Ajay Shah, look­ing even 50 years ahead, ex­pected the tools to kill mass-produced, for­mu­laic work: ro­mance nov­els churned out by the hun­dred, screen­plays, re­search pa­pers, opin­ion pieces. Great works would re­main a human pre­serve, in “a win­ner takes all world with a vengeance”.
Varma ex­pects copy­writ­ing and il­lus­tra­tion jobs to van­ish. “You don’t need a cre­ative di­rec­tor with ten copy­writ­ers. You need a cre­ative di­rec­tor who can prompt.” {002-C10}

~ Neither host feared last­ing un­em­ploy­ment. The pro­duc­tiv­ity gains will go back into the econ­omy, Varma said. The mar­ket econ­omy of the last 1,000 years ab­sorbed the steam en­gine and elec­tric­ity, Shah said, and this is “small change com­pared to that”. {#upheaval}

quote.text: So the peo­ple who are wor­ried about this are wor­ried for the wrong rea­sons.

art.caption: Amit Varma on thin and thick desire

sections.label: The fifth round
sections.head: Game on for the machines
sections.caption: machines that discover
body: What ex­cites Ajay Shah is not the chat­bot but dis­cov­ery. When a prob­lem has fixed rules and an ob­jec­tive re­ward, as chess does, a ma­chine can climb the hill and find new things in­stead of remix­ing the past. {002-C11}

AlphaZero, he said, made the hosts[[x12]] think about open­ings, sac­ri­fice and re­ward in new ways, and Magnus Carlsen changed his ideas about chess after watch­ing it. Similar meth­ods com­pre­hen­sively solved ques­tions in pro­tein fold­ing that had long de­fied human sci­ence.
## More en­gines, more va­ri­ety

Amit Varma re­called an ear­lier rev­o­lu­tion, around 2003 and 2004, when Stockfish be­came stronger than the strong­est human and play­ers began teach­ing them­selves with com­put­ers. Instead of ev­ery­thing be­com­ing ho­mogenised, “it ac­tu­ally went in the op­po­site di­rec­tion[[x11]],” he said. {002-S03}

Engines found con­crete ex­cep­tions to the Soviet school’s fixed rules about the cen­tre, space and ini­tia­tive, free­ing cre­ative play­ers such as Wesley So and Alireza Firouzja. Anand once noted that in his gen­er­a­tion a com­pletely un­ex­pected move was prob­a­bly a bad one.

~ Shah’s cau­tion was that chess is a fi­nite, closed prob­lem. Most of the world, like a car look­ing at a scene with im­per­fect in­for­ma­tion, is sta­tis­ti­cal in­fer­ence under un­cer­tainty, where there can never be a per­fect al­go­rithm.

quote.text: The beauty is chess is a fi­nite game with re­ward func­tion, and you’re able to climb that hill and dis­cover new won­ders

art.caption: Ajay Shah on machines that discover

portraits.caption: Magnus Carlsen
portraits.credit: Andreas Kontokanis from Piraeus, Greece, CC BY-SA 2.0

sections.label: The last round
sections.head: No paperclip apocalypse
sections.caption: AI alarmism and the real risks
body: Amit Varma laid out the clas­sic night­mare, the pa­per­clip max­i­mizer: an all-powerful ma­chine built to make pa­per­clips goes hay­wire and turns all or­ganic mat­ter into ma­te­rial for them, until the whole uni­verse is pa­per­clips. {002-R15}[[x13]]
He re­jected it twice. If it hap­pened, he asked, why place the human species on a pedestal? {002-C12} And it sim­ply won’t hap­pen, any more than GPS is going to de­stroy us.
Ajay Shah called ma­chine-takeover claims far­ci­cal, sci­ence-fiction ma­te­rial. When hu­mans built the au­to­mo­bile, peo­ple died in ac­ci­dents, and we blamed the driver, not the car.
## With prob­a­bil­ity one

Diagnostic ma­chines will make mis­takes and kill peo­ple, Shah said, and mil­i­tary ro­bots will kill civil­ians. “It’s going to hap­pen with prob­a­bil­ity one.” Every sys­tem trades false alarms against misses, and so­ci­ety must weigh the two. {002-C13}

Government need not do all the heavy lift­ing, Shah said: “I want to be fully Coasean.” {002-J16} His ideal for TB di­ag­no­sis is a man-machine hy­brid, with a mas­ter for the doubt­ful mid­dle cases. “But the mas­ter is ex­pen­sive,” he said, so firms will be tempted to cut cor­ners.

~ Varma added the seen and the un­seen: we see the life lost to an error, not the lives the tech­nol­ogy saves. On whether a con­scious AGI de­serves rights, Shah de­clined the premise: “I’m just not there.”

quote.text: So all en­gi­neer­ing in­volves find­ing a de­sign that finds an eth­i­cal, legal, and safe trade-off be­tween type one and type two er­rors.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on AI alarmism and the real risks

quote.text: It’s good. Lots of things are going to hap­pen and we’re going to be­come more and more ef­fec­tive. We have bet­ter ma­chines. That’s all. It’s just a con­tin­u­a­tion of the ma­chine age.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Chai, chess, code and a monster: the episode’s tales, and what they teach

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s recommendation, and the long hunt behind it
stories.head: A Chennai root in a Sahyadri cup
body: Years ago, walk­ing down a street in Chennai, Ajay Shah saw a man with a cart sell­ing some­thing he had never seen be­fore, some kind of root. He asked in English what it was. Another cus­tomer stand­ing next to him im­me­di­ately rat­tled off the plant’s sci­en­tific name: Hemidesmus in­di­cus. {#customer}

Shah bought some, wrote the name down and went home to study it. In Tamil it is nan­nari. It has hints of car­damom and cam­phor, and in Tamil Nadu it is made into a syrup, often with way too much sugar.

Then, a cou­ple of years ago, Shah was hik­ing in the Sahyadris near a place called Jivdan. A vil­lage woman was mak­ing chai, and he asked for gin­ger. She had none, and of­fered some­thing else. She brought back a masala chai un­like any he had tasted. {#jivdan}

Shah, who loves masala chai and is al­ways ex­per­i­ment­ing with recipes, wanted to be sure he never lost it. So he made a voice record­ing of the woman and her hus­band say­ing the root’s Marathi name. {#recording}
The hus­band dug him a sapling from the hill­side: “Take some home for the wife.”

None of Shah’s Marathi-speaking friends had heard the name. Then one day, smelling the root, he made the con­nec­tion. “I had that aha mo­ment that this smell re­minds me of Nannari, the Tamilian root that I had pur­chased in Chennai,” he said. {002-S08}
~ He tri­an­gu­lated, and it was the same root. Later he found a Tamil Muslim tea recipe that uses it. His ad­vice: grind nan­nari to a pow­der and put it in your chai.
stories.why: Local knowl­edge is scat­tered across lan­guages and re­gions. A voice record­ing, a sapling and a good nose turned two trips, years apart, into one story, and one novel cup of masala chai.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma, no tea drinker, has had Shah’s herbal tea some thirty times. Susan, Shah’s wife, says it isn’t tea: there’s no tea in it. {#susan}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on nannari, the root in his chai

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the engine that taught itself chess
stories.head: Centuries of chess in a day
body: In 2017, Amit Varma said, AlphaZero taught it­self chess[[x14]] in twenty-four hours, with no human data­base, sim­ply by play­ing against it­self. {#selftaught}

Its games fol­lowed the same path as humanity’s. It took up the French Defence, fash­ion­able in the 19th cen­tury and now known to be sub­op­ti­mal. It dis­cov­ered the Berlin Defence, which Kramnik un­leashed, Varma said, in 2001. {#berlin} Then it went be­yond us, re­think­ing ma­te­rial against ini­tia­tive and at­tack­ing down the a- and h-files, as Magnus Carlsen later did.
Carlsen’s coach, Peter Heine Nielsen, said: “I al­ways won­dered that if aliens with a su­pe­rior in­tel­li­gence came to Earth, how would they play chess? And now I know.” {002-S04}
~ Ajay Shah drew his own les­son: there is no need to win back a sac­ri­ficed pawn in two or three moves. “It’s okay, take 15 moves.” {#fifteen}

quote.text: It’s an alien in­tel­li­gence. It is a black box.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on AlphaZero’s alien chess

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on machines that improve machines
stories.head: Teaching old algorithms new tricks
body: For about 50 years, Ajay Shah said, the best way to mul­ti­ply ma­tri­ces was the Strassen al­go­rithm, and in all that time no human had found a way to do bet­ter. {#strassen}

Then sci­en­tists turned the prob­lem into a game. They rep­re­sented the al­go­rithm it­self as a pa­ram­e­ter vec­tor and op­ti­mised it for cor­rect­ness and speed. The re­sult was the first im­prove­ments in 50 years, now going into com­puter sys­tems all over the world.
DeepMind did the same for sort­ing code in LLVM, pe­nal­is­ing mis­takes and slow­ness, and today we hold bet­ter codes for sort­ing. {002-R12}
~ Readers of sci­ence fic­tion, Shah noted, have long imag­ined ma­chines that help us make bet­ter ma­chines, in a spi­ral all the way to the sin­gu­lar­ity. “Well, here we are.” {002-S05}
stories.why: Even computing’s most basic op­er­a­tions had room to im­prove. The spi­ral of ma­chines build­ing bet­ter ma­chines has begun, Shah said, and it part­ners with human re­search: math­e­ma­ti­cians now try to prove the­o­rems about what the ma­chines found.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma’s reply: any­one who has seen him wrap bacon round a sausage knows he is “bloody good at pro­tein fold­ing”. {002-J04}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on machines that make better machines

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Mary Wollstonecraft’s daughter
stories.head: The novel no model could write
body: The baby whose birth killed Mary Wollstonecraft grew up, mar­ried Percy Shelley and be­came Mary Shelley. Otherwise, Amit Varma said, she would have been Mary Wollstonecraft II.

In her early twen­ties, he said, she wrote *Frankenstein*[[x15]], whose mon­ster has be­come a metaphor for many mod­ern fears about AI. {002-R19} People call it the first sci­ence fic­tion book; Varma prefers “proto-science fic­tion”. Its craft can be cri­tiqued with a mod­ern lens, but there was noth­ing like it be­fore.
Varma tied it back to the episode’s ar­gu­ment. “If you imag­ine her LLM, there is noth­ing like that. She’s just cre­at­ing this new genre, sui generis.” {002-S07}
~ Read the mother’s book and then the daughter’s, he said, and the arc is fas­ci­nat­ing. For the whole story he rec­om­mended Charlotte Gordon’s *Romantic Outlaws*[[x16]]. {002-R20}
stories.why: A model trained only on what came be­fore, Varma sug­gested, would not have writ­ten *Frankenstein*. From the mother’s “Why not women also?” to the daughter’s mon­ster, two lives show what gen­uinely new cre­ation looks like.

quiz.q: Which Bruce Springsteen song gave the show its name, and what is it about?
quiz.a: *You’re Missing*, about an apart­ment after a loved one died in 9/11.

quiz.q: Which theory, Ajay Shah argued, could no LLM with every text of 1905 invent?
quiz.a: Einstein’s spe­cial the­ory of rel­a­tiv­ity: a cor­pus with­out it can­not pro­duce it.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s quartile model, what can an LLM do for a Q2 worker?
quiz.a: Lift them to roughly Q3 work, as long as a mas­ter ap­proves it.

quiz.q: What did Carlsen’s coach Peter Heine Nielsen say AlphaZero had finally shown him?
quiz.a: How aliens with a su­pe­rior in­tel­li­gence would play chess if they came to Earth.

quiz.q: Why, according to Amit Varma, did Mary Wollstonecraft die after giving birth?
quiz.a: An in­fec­tion: doc­tors did not yet know they had to wash their hands.

quiz.q: Where did Ajay Shah first meet nannari, and where did he taste it in chai?
quiz.a: From a cart on a Chennai street; in a vil­lage near Jivdan.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 2. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Mary Shelley (Richard Rothwell, public domain); Albert Einstein (Ferdinand Schmutzer / Adam Cuerden, public domain); Mary Wollstonecraft (John Opie, public domain); Magnus Carlsen (Andreas Kontokanis from Piraeus, Greece, CC BY-SA 2.0); Bruce Springsteen (Raph_PH, CC BY 4.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Apple.

shelf.title: You’re Missing
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: The Springsteen song that gave the show its name and world­view: its line ‘ev­ery­thing is everything’ points at all the world’s won­ders while mark­ing someone’s ab­sence.

shelf.title: Do Not Go Gentle Into That Good Night
shelf.creator: Dylan Thomas
shelf.why: He uses it as the con­trast to his own stance: not rag­ing against the world, but a quiet, con­fi­dent, cu­ri­ous en­gage­ment with it.

shelf.title: A Small-Sized Mystery
shelf.creator: Jane Hirshfield
shelf.why: A com­pan­ion piece to the episode’s point that much about human be­ings re­mains a mys­tery.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah on how LLMs will impact us
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The longer writ­ten ver­sion of his view: LLMs are use­ful word-prediction tools that need a master’s over­sight, not in­tel­li­gence.

shelf.title: The War Against Cliche
shelf.creator: Martin Amis
shelf.why: A great col­lec­tion of Amis’s crit­i­cism.

shelf.title: In a Silent Way (Episode 316 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Gaurav Chintamani
shelf.why: Musician Gaurav Chintamani on how a big hit can be­come a curse (you keep chang­ing, but au­di­ences keep shout­ing for a three-minute song from twenty years ago) and on whether orig­i­nal­ity even ex­ists.

shelf.title: The dialect of a cricket writer (2005)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: His own cat­a­logue of how sportswrit­ing runs on stock phrases: human au­to­com­plete in ac­tion.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Jerry Pinto (Episode 314 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Jerry Pinto
shelf.why: An eight-and-a-half-hour oral his­tory that Amit calls per­haps his most mem­o­rable, and the episode through which many lis­ten­ers find the show.

shelf.title: Murder in Mahim
shelf.creator: Jerry Pinto
shelf.why: He calls it a beau­ti­ful crime thriller.

shelf.title: This century and the last one: A report card for the first 10 years (2010)
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s own long-horizon look at how the cen­tury was going.

shelf.title: Discovering faster matrix multiplication algorithms with reinforcement learning
shelf.creator: Alhussein Fawzi & others
shelf.why: It pro­duced the first im­prove­ments in about 50 years to one of computing’s most basic op­er­a­tions, by turn­ing al­go­rithm de­sign into a game.

shelf.title: AlphaDev discovers faster sorting algorithms
shelf.creator: DeepMind
shelf.why: It shows ma­chines find­ing bet­ter code for some­thing as fun­da­men­tal as sort­ing, which then feeds back into stronger ma­chines.

shelf.title: The New World Upon Us (2017)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: His fuller ac­count of why AlphaZero’s self-taught chess was a turn­ing point.

shelf.title: Google’s AlphaZero Destroys Stockfish In 100-Game Match
shelf.creator: Mike Klein
shelf.why: The con­tem­po­rary re­port on the match that made AlphaZero fa­mous.

shelf.title: The Paperclip Maximizer
shelf.why: An ex­plainer of the sce­nario in which a ma­chine built to max­imise pa­per­clips turns ev­ery­thing into pa­per­clips.

shelf.title: Why AI Will Save the World
shelf.creator: Marc Andreeson
shelf.why: In Amit’s words, a beau­ti­ful essay that ad­dresses all of these ques­tions in great de­tail.

shelf.title: When We Were Robots in Egypt
shelf.creator: Jo Walton
shelf.why: A lit­er­ary take on the ma­chines-take-over theme he finds far­ci­cal as a fore­cast but beau­ti­ful as art.

shelf.title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
shelf.creator: Mary Wollstonecraft
shelf.why: The found­ing protofem­i­nist text, writ­ten with no role mod­els: it ap­plies Locke’s nat­u­ral rights to women, ar­gues that a false ed­u­ca­tion makes women slaves of the male gaze and grounds virtue in rea­son.

shelf.title: Frankenstein
shelf.creator: Mary Shelley
shelf.why: Written with no genre or craft mod­els to fol­low, a pi­o­neer­ing work of proto-science fic­tion with an in­no­va­tive nested struc­ture of three nar­ra­tors.

shelf.title: Romantic Outlaws
shelf.creator: Charlotte Gordon
shelf.why: A joint bi­og­ra­phy of Mary Wollstonecraft and her daugh­ter Mary Shelley, beau­ti­ful and in­spir­ing lives that show how hos­tile their world was to women: an­i­mals gained legal pro­tec­tion twenty years be­fore the first law lim­it­ing vi­o­lence against women.

shelf.title: The poetry of Mary Oliver
shelf.creator: Mary Oliver
shelf.why: What schools should be teach­ing in­stead of the Romantic poets.

shelf.title: The poetry of Mark Strand
shelf.creator: Mark Strand
shelf.why: The other poet he would teach in­stead.

shelf.title: Amit Varma’s Book Club episodes on A Vindication of the Rights of Woman and Frankenstein (Storytel)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s short audio in­tro­duc­tion, made for Storytel, to Mary Wollstonecraft’s A Vindication of the Rights of Woman: how one of his great he­roes ex­tended Locke’s rights to women and so began mod­ern fem­i­nism.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

shelf.title: Saaya & the Rituals of Tamil Muslim Milk Tea
shelf.creator: Maazin Buhari
shelf.why: The source for the recipe be­hind his ‘bet­ter masala chai’.

shelf.title: Nannari root (Amrutmul, Hemidesmus indicus)
shelf.why: It gives a novel, unique flavour with hints of car­damom and cam­phor that most masala-chai lovers north of Karnataka have never tried.

laughs.text: Told by the pro­ducer to drop his ‘rest­ing pout face’, Amit prom­ises a ‘jok­er­ish per­ma­nent smile’ for the rest of the episode. Then Ajay: ‘Maybe a joker mask will work.’
Amit: ‘we of course are artists as we dis­cussed in the last episode. That was an al­le­ga­tion made on us.’

Ajay imag­ines an LLM read­ing ev­ery­thing the two hosts have writ­ten, guess­ing ‘that we are nutcases’, and ar­riv­ing at the name Everything is Everything. That, he says, would be the pin­na­cle of word pre­dic­tion.

Amit on pro­tein fold­ing: ‘if you’ve ever seen me wrap a piece of bacon around a sausage, you’ll re­al­ize I’m bloody good at pro­tein fold­ing.’ He then asks Ajay, who had de­scribed ‘squeal­ing with excitement’, to ac­tu­ally demon­strate a squeal.
Amit on Mary Wollstonecraft: ‘Married to an in­ter­est­ing guy, also a bit of an ass­hole, but leave him out of the equa­tion.’
Amit closes the AI de­bate: they ‘agree to dis­agree ge­nially, as AI also would, be­cause no emo­tions — we are the messed up crea­tures.’
Ajay’s wife Susan says his herbal ‘tea’ isn’t tea at all, be­cause there’s no tea in it.
Hemingway, quoted by Ajay on the craft of writ­ing: ‘a good day is one in which you write one good sen­tence.’

Ken Thompson’s dy­namic-programming al­go­rithm for chess endgames. Ajay: it was ‘like a thun­der­bolt going off’ when it ar­rived and is ‘boring’ today, an eerie thing that ‘looks 20 deep with­out need­ing 20 ply.’
Idealism vs ma­te­ri­al­ism: Ajay puts him­self ‘on the ma­te­ri­al­ism side. There is noth­ing hap­pen­ing in the skull other than some quan­tum me­chan­ics of how the atoms in this brain work.’
Ajay’s ar­chi­tec­ture anal­ogy: a model stand­ing at Akbar’s tomb in Sikandra would never in­vent the Taj Mahal, the next step in ‘the great arms race of monuments’.
Amit, de­flat­ing human ex­cep­tion­al­ism: ‘some would of course argue we are col­o­nized by bac­te­ria, we’re col­o­nized by wheat.’
Ajay: if you grant con­scious AGI, ‘then we’re build­ing von Neumann ma­chines. We’re col­o­niz­ing the gal­axy.’
Ajay on AI reg­u­la­tion: ‘I want to be fully Coasean. You don’t have to have gov­ern­ments doing all the heavy lift­ing.’

Amit’s hot take on the Romantic poets Shelley, Byron and Keats: they ‘should not even be taught in school’ be­cause ‘they take away young people’s pas­sion for po­etry. They’re not even good poets, we ro­man­ti­cize them.’
